Following its founding, RCA acted as the sales agent for a small line of Westinghouse and GE branded receivers and parts used by home constructors, originally for a limited market of [amateur radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amateur_radio "Amateur radio") enthusiasts. By 1922, the rise of broadcasting had dramatically increased the demand for radio equipment by the general public, and this development was reflected in the title of RCA's June 1, 1922, catalog, "Radio Enters the Home". RCA began selling receivers under the "Radiola" name, marketing equipment produced by GE and Westinghouse under the production agreement that allocated a 60%–40% ratio in output between the two companies. Although the patent cross-licensing agreements had been intended to give the participants domination of equipment sales, the tremendous growth of the market led to fierce competition, and in 1925 RCA fell behind [Atwater Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atwater_Kent "Atwater Kent") as the leader in receiver sales. RCA was particularly hamstrung by the need to coordinate its sales within the limits of the GE/Westinghouse production quotas, and often had difficulty keeping up with industry trends. However, the company made a key advance in early 1924 when it began selling the first [superheterodyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superheterodyne "Superheterodyne") receivers, whose high level of performance increased the brand's reputation and popularity. RCA was the exclusive manufacturer of superheterodyne radio sets until 1930. All RCA receivers were battery powered until late 1927 when plug-in AC sets were introduced, providing another boost in sales.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-26)

## Vacuum tubes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=RCA_Corporation&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Vacuum tubes")]

[![Image 28](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/RCA_OA2.JPG/250px-RCA_OA2.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:RCA_OA2.JPG)

RCA voltage regulator vacuum tube

RCA inherited American Marconi's status as a major producer of vacuum tubes, which were branded **Radiotron** in the United States. Especially after the rise of broadcasting, they were a major profit source for the company. RCA's strong patent position meant that the company effectively set the selling prices for vacuum tubes in the U.S., which were significantly higher than in Europe, where [Lee de Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_de_Forest "Lee de Forest") had allowed a key patent to lapse.

The company began work on a secret project for the U.S. Navy called Madame X in September 1942. The Bloomington, Indiana, plant was one of the first of five RCA plants to produce Madame X vacuum tubes, which included a [proximity fuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proximity_fuse "Proximity fuse") used to electronically detonate its payload when it was in range of its target, as opposed to relying on a direct hit. James V. Forrestal, former secretary of the Navy said, "The proximity fuse had helped blaze the trail to Japan. Without the protection this ingenious device has given the surface ships of the fleet, our westward push could not have been so swift and the cost in men and ships would have been immeasurably greater."[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-27)

RCA was responsible for creating a series of innovative products, ranging from [octal base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octal_tube "Octal tube") metal tubes co-developed with [General Electric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Electric "General Electric") before World War II, to greatly miniaturized [Nuvistor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuvistor "Nuvistor") tubes, used in the tuners of the New Vista series of television receivers. The Nuvistors were a last major vacuum tube innovation, along with General Electric's [Compactron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compactron "Compactron"), and were meant to compete with the newly introduced transistor. By 1975, RCA had completely switched from tubes to solid-state devices in their television sets, except for the [Cathode-ray tube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathode-ray_tube "Cathode-ray tube") (CRT) picture tube itself.

## Phonographs and records

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=RCA_Corporation&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Phonographs and records")]

See also: [RCA Victor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Victor "RCA Victor")

The rapid rise of radio broadcasting during the early 1920s, which provided unlimited free entertainment in the home, had a detrimental effect on the American phonograph record industry. The [Victor Talking Machine Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Talking_Machine_Company "Victor Talking Machine Company") in [Camden, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camden,_New_Jersey "Camden, New Jersey"), was then the world's largest manufacturer of [phonographs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phonographs "Phonographs") and [records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phonograph_record "Phonograph record"), including its popular line of "Victrola" console and tabletop phonographs. In January 1929, RCA purchased the Victor Talking Machine Company; this acquisition became known as the **RCA Victor** Division of the Radio Corporation of America, and included ownership of Victor's Japanese subsidiary, the [Victor Company of Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Company_of_Japan "Victor Company of Japan") (JVC), formed in 1927 and controlling interest in [The Gramophone Company Ltd.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gramophone_Company "The Gramophone Company") (later [EMI Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EMI_Records "EMI Records")) in England.

RCA's acquisition of the Victor company included the rights to the iconic [Nipper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nipper "Nipper")/"[His Master's Voice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/His_Master's_Voice "His Master's Voice")" trademark across the Western Hemisphere.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-28) RCA Victor popularized combined radio receiver-phonographs, and also created [RCA Photophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Photophone "RCA Photophone"), a movie [sound-on-film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound-on-film "Sound-on-film") system that competed with [William Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Fox_(producer) "William Fox (producer)")'s sound-on-film [Movietone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movietone_sound_system "Movietone sound system") and [Warner Bros.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros. "Warner Bros.")' [sound-on-disc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound-on-disc "Sound-on-disc")[Vitaphone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitaphone "Vitaphone"). Although early announcements of the merger between RCA and Victor stressed that the two firms were linking on equal terms to form a new company, RCA initially had little interest in the phonograph record business. RCA's management was interested essentially in Victor's superior sales capabilities through the record company's large network of authorized distributors and dealers, as well as the extensive, efficient manufacturing facilities in [Camden, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camden,_New_Jersey "Camden, New Jersey"). Immediately following the purchase of Victor, RCA began planning the manufacture of radio sets and components on Victor's Camden assembly lines, while gradually decreasing the production of Victrolas and records.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-29)

Following the [Stock market crash of 1929](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stock_market_crash_of_1929 "Stock market crash of 1929") and subsequent [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression"), the entire phonograph record industry in America nearly foundered. During the nadir of the record business in the early 1930s, the manufacture of phonographs and records had all but ceased; extant older phonographs were now considered obsolete and most had been relegated to the attic or basement. In 1930, RCA Victor began selling the first all-electric Victrola and in 1931, the company attempted to revitalize moribund record sales with the introduction of 33 1⁄3[revolutions-per-minute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutions_per_minute "Revolutions per minute") (rpm) long play records, which were a commercial failure during the Great Depression, partly because the Victrolas with two speed turntables required to play them were exorbitantly expensive, and also because the audio performance of the new records was generally poor; the new format used the same groove size as existing 78 rpm records,[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-30) and it would require the smaller-radius stylus of the later microgroove systems to achieve acceptable slower-speed performance. Additionally, the new long-play records were pressed in a pliable, vinyl-based material called "Victrolac" which wore out rapidly under the weight of heavy magnetic pickups and tonearms then in use.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-31)

In 1934, following the debacle of its long-play record, RCA Victor introduced the Duo Jr., an inexpensive, small, basic electric turntable designed to be plugged into radio sets. The Duo Jr. was sold at cost, but was discounted even further with the purchase of a certain number of Victor records. The Duo Jr.'s rock-bottom price and America's slowly improving economy helped to overcome the national apathy to phonographs, and record sales gradually began to recover.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-32) Around 1935, RCA began marketing the modern RCA Victor M Special, a polished aluminum portable record player designed by [John Vassos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Vassos "John Vassos") that has become an icon of 1930s American industrial design.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-33) In 1949, RCA Victor released the first 45 rpm "single" records, as a response to [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records") successful introduction of its microgroove 33 1⁄3 rpm "[LP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LP_record "LP record")" format in 1948. As RCA Victor adopted Columbia's 33 1⁄3 rpm LP records in 1950,[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-34)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-35) Columbia then adopted RCA Victor's 45 rpm records.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-36)

In 1965, RCA Victor launched the [8-track tape cartridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/8-track_tape "8-track tape"). For over a decade, sales of 8-tracks made a huge and profitable impact on consumers of recorded music. Sales of the 8-track format began to decline during the late 1970s as consumer preference turned to the [compact cassette tape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_cassette_tape "Compact cassette tape") introduced by [Philips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philips "Philips") in 1963. By 1982, 8-track tapes were no longer being stocked by most music retailers and by 1990, the format had vanished completely.

## Motion pictures

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=RCA_Corporation&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Motion pictures")]

RCA also made investments in the movie industry, but they performed poorly. In April 1928, RCA Photophone, Inc., was organized by a group of companies including RCA to develop sound-movie technology. In the fall of 1927, RCA had purchased stock in Film Booking Office (FBO), and on October 25, 1928, with the help of [Joseph P. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_P._Kennedy "Joseph P. Kennedy"), the [Radio-Keith-Orpheum Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RKO_Pictures "RKO Pictures") (RKO) studio was formed by merging FBO with Keith-Albee-Orpheum Corporation (KAO), a company whose holdings included motion picture theaters. The theaters in which RKO had an interest provided a potential market for the RCA Photophone sound systems. RCA ownership of RKO stock expanded from about one quarter in 1930 to about 61% in 1932.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-37) RKO encountered severe financial problems, going into receivership from early 1933 until 1940. RCA sold its holdings in the studio to raise funds for its basic operations.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Separation from General Electric

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=RCA_Corporation&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Separation from General Electric")]

After years of industry complaints that the cross-licensing agreements between RCA, GE, and Westinghouse had in effect created illegal monopolies, the U.S. Department of Justice brought antitrust charges against the three companies in May 1930.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-38) After much negotiation, in 1932 the Justice Department accepted a consent agreement that removed the restrictions established by the cross-licensing agreements, and also provided that RCA would become a fully independent company. As a result, GE and Westinghouse gave up their ownership interests in RCA, while RCA was allowed to keep its factories.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-39) To give RCA a chance to establish itself, GE and Westinghouse were required to refrain from competing in the radio business for the next two and one-half years.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-40) In 1954, the Justice Department filed a major antitrust lawsuit against RCA, with charges including patent monopolization, illegal cross-licensing with GE, Westinghouse and AT&T and anticompetitive harassment. The 1958 consent decree forced RCA to share its television and radio patents with domestic competitors on a royalty-free basis. [[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-FOOTNOTESobel1986-41)

## Television

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=RCA_Corporation&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Television")]

See also: [History of television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_television "History of television")

[![Image 29](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/1939_RCA_Television_Advertisement.jpg/250px-1939_RCA_Television_Advertisement.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1939_RCA_Television_Advertisement.jpg)

RCA ad for the beginning, in April 1939, of regular experimental television broadcasting by RCA-NBC over New York City station W2XBS (forerunner of today's WNBC/4), for "an hour at a time, twice a week."[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-42)

RCA began television development in early 1929, after an overly optimistic [Vladimir K. Zworykin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_K._Zworykin "Vladimir K. Zworykin") convinced Sarnoff that a commercial version of his prototype system could be produced in a relatively short time for $100,000. Following what would actually be many years of additional research and millions of dollars, RCA demonstrated an all-electronic black-and-white television system at the [1939 New York World's Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1939_New_York_World's_Fair "1939 New York World's Fair"). RCA began regular experimental television broadcasting from the NBC studios to the New York metropolitan area on April 30, 1939, via station W2XBS, [channel 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Channel_1_(North_American_TV) "Channel 1 (North American TV)") (which evolved into [WNBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WNBC "WNBC") channel 4) from the new [Empire State Building transmitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_State_Building#Broadcast_stations "Empire State Building") on top of the structure. Around this time, RCA began selling its first television set models, including the TRK-5 and TRK-9, in various New York stores.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-43) However, the FCC had not approved the start of commercial television operations, because technical standards had not yet been finalized. Concerned that RCA's broadcasts were an attempt to flood the market with sets that would force it to adopt RCA's current technology, the FCC stepped in to limit its broadcasts.

Following the adoption of [National Television System Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Television_System_Committee "National Television System Committee") (NTSC) recommended standards, the FCC authorized the start of commercial television broadcasts on July 1, 1941. The entry of the United States into World War II a few months later greatly slowed its deployment, but RCA resumed selling television receivers almost immediately after the war ended in 1945.

In 1950, the FCC adopted a standard for [color television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television "Color television") that had been promoted by CBS, but the effort soon failed, primarily because the color broadcasts could not be received by existing black-and-white sets. As the result of a major research push, RCA engineers developed a method of "compatible" color transmissions that, through the use of interlacing, simultaneously broadcast color and black-and-white images, which could be picked up by both color and existing black-and-white sets. In 1953, RCA's all-electronic color television technology was adopted as the standard for the United States. At that time, Sarnoff predicted annual color television sales would reach 1.78 million in 1956, but the receivers were expensive and difficult to adjust, and there was initially a lack of color programming, so sales lagged badly and the actual 1956 total would only be 120,000.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-44) RCA's ownership of NBC proved to be a major benefit, as that network was instructed to promote its color program offerings; even so, it was not until 1968 that color television sales in the United States surpassed those of black-and-white sets.

While lauding the technical prowess of his RCA engineers who had developed color television, David Sarnoff, in marked contrast to William Paley, president of CBS, did not disguise his dislike for popular television programs. His authorized biography even boasted that "no one has yet caught him in communion with one of the upper dozen or so top-rated programs" and "The popular programs, to put the matter bluntly, have very little appeal for him."[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-45)

RCA [professional video cameras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professional_video_camera "Professional video camera") and studio gear, particularly of the [TK-40/41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TK-40/41 "TK-40/41") series, became standard equipment at many American television network affiliates, as RCA [CT-100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CT-100 "CT-100")[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-46) ("RCA Merrill" to dealers) television sets introduced color television to the public.

## Diversification

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=RCA_Corporation&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Diversification")]

[![Image 30](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/Sarnoff_RCA_videotape_recorder_1954.jpg/250px-Sarnoff_RCA_videotape_recorder_1954.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sarnoff_RCA_videotape_recorder_1954.jpg)

David Sarnoff with the first RCA videotape recorder, 1954

[![Image 31](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/RCA_Video-Aufzeichnungsger%C3%A4t.jpg/250px-RCA_Video-Aufzeichnungsger%C3%A4t.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:RCA_Video-Aufzeichnungsger%C3%A4t.jpg)

RCA Television Quad head 2-inch color recorder-reproducer used at broadcast studios from the late-1960s to the early 1980s[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-47)

In 1941, shortly before the United States entered World War II, the cornerstone was laid for a research and development facility in [Princeton, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton,_New_Jersey "Princeton, New Jersey") called RCA Laboratories. Led for many years by [Elmer Engstrom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elmer_Engstrom "Elmer Engstrom"), it was used to develop many innovations, including [color television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television "Color television"), the [electron microscope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron_microscope "Electron microscope"), [CMOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CMOS "CMOS")-based technology, [heterojunction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heterojunction "Heterojunction") physics, [optoelectronic emitting devices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light-emitting_diode#Discoveries_and_early_devices "Light-emitting diode"), [liquid crystal displays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_crystal_display "Liquid crystal display") (LCDs), [videocassette recorders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Videocassette_recorder "Videocassette recorder"), [direct broadcast television, direct broadcast satellite systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct-broadcast_satellite "Direct-broadcast satellite") and [high-definition television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-definition_television "High-definition television").

RCA plants switched to war production shortly after the U.S. entered the war in December 1941. During World War II, RCA was involved in [radar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radar "Radar") and radio development in support of the war effort, and ranked 43rd among United States corporations in the value of wartime military production contracts.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-48) One such contract was to outfit the battleship [USS Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Texas "USS Texas") with a 400-megahertz pulse radar set, using technology developed by RCA acoustics scientist, [Irving Wolff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irving_Wolff "Irving Wolff").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-49) During and after the war, RCA set up several new divisions for defense, space exploration and other activities. The RCA Service Corporation provided large numbers of staff for the [Distant Early Warning (DEW) Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distant_Early_Warning_Line "Distant Early Warning Line"). RCA units won five [Army–Navy "E" Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army%E2%80%93Navy_%22E%22_Award "Army–Navy \"E\" Award") for Excellence in production.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-50) Due to the hostilities between Japan and the United States during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), the [Victor Company of Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Company_of_Japan "Victor Company of Japan") became an independent company after seceding from RCA Victor in the United States; JVC retained the 'Victor' and "His Master's Voice" trademarks for use in Japan only.

In 1955, RCA sold its Estate brand of large appliance operations to [Whirlpool Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whirlpool_Corporation "Whirlpool Corporation"). As part of this transaction, Whirlpool was given the right to market "RCA Whirlpool" appliances through the mid-1960s.

RCA Graphic Systems Division (GSD) was an early supplier of electronics designed for the printing and publishing industries. It contracted with German company [Rudolf Hell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Hell "Rudolf Hell") to market adaptations of the Digiset photocomposition system as the Videocomp, and a Laser Color Scanner. The Videocomp was supported by a Spectra computer that ran the Page-1 and, later the Page-II and FileComp composition systems. RCA later sold the Videocomp rights to [Information International Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_International_Inc. "Information International Inc.")

## Computers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=RCA_Corporation&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Computers")]

See also: [Computing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computing "Computing")

RCA was one of a number of companies in the 1960s that entered the mainframe computer field to challenge the market leader [International Business Machines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Business_Machines "International Business Machines") (IBM). Although at this time computers were almost universally used for routine data processing and scientific research, in 1964 Sarnoff, who prided himself as a visionary, predicted that "The computer will become the hub of a vast network of remote data stations and information banks feeding into the machine at a transmission rate of a billion or more bits of information a second... Eventually, a global communications network handling voice, data and facsimile will instantly link man to machine—or machine to machine—by land, air, underwater, and space circuits. [The computer] will affect man's ways of thinking, his means of education, his relationship to his physical and social environment, and it will alter his ways of living. ...[Before the end of this century, these forces] will coalesce into what unquestionably will become the greatest adventure of the human mind."[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-51)

RCA marketed a [Spectra 70](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectra_70 "Spectra 70") computer line that was hardware, but not software, compatible with IBM's [System/360](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System/360 "System/360") series. It also produced the RCA Series, which competed against the [IBM System/370](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM_System/370 "IBM System/370").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-52) This technology was leased to the [English Electric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Electric "English Electric") company, which used it for their System 4 series, which were essentially RCA Spectra 70 clones. RCA's TSOS operating system was the first mainframe, demand paging, virtual memory operating system on the market. By 1971, despite a significant investment, RCA had only a 4% market share, and it was estimated that it would cost around $500 million over the next five years to remain competitive with the IBM/370 series. On September 17, 1971, the RCA board of directors announced its decision to close its computer systems division (RCA-CSD), which would be written off as a $490 million company loss. [Sperry Rand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sperry_Corporation "Sperry Corporation")'s UNIVAC division took over the RCA computer division in January 1972. Univac did not want the Spectra computers because they were similar to its own 9000 series; instead, they wanted RCA's computer customer base.

## Later years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=RCA_Corporation&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Later years")]

[![Image 32](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/Edgar_H._Griffiths%2C_RCA_Annual_Meeting%2C_NYC.jpg/250px-Edgar_H._Griffiths%2C_RCA_Annual_Meeting%2C_NYC.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Edgar_H._Griffiths,_RCA_Annual_Meeting,_NYC.jpg)

Edgar H. Griffiths, RCA president from 1976 to 1981, at the 1979 Annual Meeting, NYC

On January 1, 1965, Robert Sarnoff succeeded his father as RCA's president, although the elder Sarnoff remained in control as chairman of the board. The younger Sarnoff sought to modernize RCA's image with the introduction in late 1968 of what was then a futuristic-looking new logo (the letters 'RCA' in block, modernized form), replacing the original lightning bolt logo, and the virtual retirement of both the Victor and Nipper/"His Master's Voice" trademarks. The RCA Victor Division was renamed [RCA Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Records "RCA Records"); the 'Victor' and 'Victrola' trademarks were no longer used on RCA consumer electronics. 'Victor' was now restricted to the labels and album covers of RCA's regular popular record releases, while the Nipper/"His Master's Voice" trademark was seen only on the album covers of [Red Seal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Red_Seal "RCA Red Seal") records.

In 1969, the company name was officially changed from Radio Corporation of America to the "RCA Corporation", to reflect its broader range of corporate activities and expansion into other countries. At the end of that same year, David Sarnoff, after being incapacitated by a long-term illness, was removed as the company's chairman of the board. He died in December 1971.

RCA's exit from the mainframe computer market in 1971 marked a milestone in its transition from electronics and technology toward Robert Sarnoff's goal to diversify RCA as a multinational business [conglomerate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conglomerate_(company) "Conglomerate (company)"). During the late 1960s and 1970s, the company made a wide-ranging series of acquisitions, including [Hertz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hertz_Corporation "The Hertz Corporation") (rental cars), [Banquet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banquet_Foods "Banquet Foods") (frozen foods and [TV dinners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TV_dinner "TV dinner")), [Coronet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaulieu_International_Group "Beaulieu International Group") (carpeting), [Random House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_House "Random House") (publishing) and [Gibson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Greetings "American Greetings") (greeting cards). However, the company was slipping into financial disarray, with wags calling it "Rugs Chickens & Automobiles" (RCA), to poke fun at its new direction.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-Chickens-53)

During this period, RCA continued to maintain its high standards of engineering excellence in broadcast and satellite communications equipment, but profits generated by the NBC television and radio networks began to decline.

Robert Sarnoff's tenure as RCA president was unsuccessful, marked by falling profits. While out of the country in October 1975, Sarnoff was ousted in a "[boardroom coup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boardroom_coup "Boardroom coup")" led by Anthony Conrad, who became RCA's new president. Conrad resigned less than a year later after he admitted failing to file income tax returns for six years. His successor, Edgar H. Griffiths, proved to be unpopular and retired in early 1981. Griffiths was succeeded by Thornton Bradshaw, who turned out to be the last RCA president.

After the departure of Robert Sarnoff, Griffiths, who considered the demoted "His Master's Voice" trademark a "valuable company asset", restored Nipper as RCA's corporate mascot. On October 31, 1976, RCA formally announced the return of the Nipper trademark to RCA products and advertising. Earlier that year, RCA Records had begun to reinstate Nipper to most record labels in countries and territories where RCA held the rights to the trademark. Once again, Nipper was widely used in RCA newspaper, magazine, and TV advertisements. The trademark also returned to company stationery, sales literature, shipping cartons, store displays, delivery and service vehicles and reappeared on RCA television sets and in 1981, the new [CED Videodisc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CED_Videodisc "CED Videodisc") system. Several newspaper articles and TV news reports about Nipper's revival appeared at the time. A multitude of new Nipper promotional items and collectibles also appeared, including T-shirts, caps, neckties, beach towels, cigarette lighters, coin banks, keychains, watches, clocks, coffee mugs, drinking glasses and stuffed toys.

Projects attempting to establish new [consumer electronics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consumer_electronics "Consumer electronics") products during this era failed and lost RCA much money and prestige. An [RCA Studio II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Studio_II "RCA Studio II") home video game console, introduced in 1977, was canceled just under two years later due to poor sales. Development of RCA's [capacitance electronic (CED) videodisc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capacitance_Electronic_Disc "Capacitance Electronic Disc") system began in 1964, and after several years of delays was launched in March 1981. Marketed under the [SelectaVision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SelectaVision "SelectaVision") name, the RCA CED videodisc system represented the largest investment RCA made in a single product, even greater than color TV. However, the system was practically obsolete by the time it finally appeared, and never reached the manufacturing volumes needed to bring its price down to the level needed to compete against the newer, recordable and increasingly cheaper videotape technology. In April 1984, after three years of slow sales, RCA abandoned manufacture of the CED players, and ended videodisc production in 1986, after a loss of around $650 million.

Around 1980, RCA corporate strategy reported on moving manufacture of its television receivers to Mexico. In 1981, [Columbia Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Pictures "Columbia Pictures") sold its share in the home video division to RCA and outside of North America this division was renamed "RCA/Columbia Pictures International Video (now [Sony Pictures Home Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Pictures_Home_Entertainment "Sony Pictures Home Entertainment"))". The following year, within North America, it was renamed to "[RCA/Columbia Pictures Home Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA/Columbia_Pictures_Home_Video "RCA/Columbia Pictures Home Video")". In 1983, the German media conglomerate [Bertelsmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertelsmann "Bertelsmann") sold 50% of [Arista Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arista_Records "Arista Records") to RCA Records; in 1985, RCA and Bertelsmann formed a joint venture, RCA/Ariola International, which took over management of RCA Records. Bertelsmann would fully acquire RCA Records from General Electric after GE absorbed RCA in 1986.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-bertelsmann.com-54)

RCA was still profitable in 1983, when it switched manufacturing of its VHS VCRs from [Panasonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panasonic "Panasonic") to [Hitachi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hitachi "Hitachi"). In 1984, RCA Broadcast Systems Division moved from the RCA Victor plant in [Camden, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camden,_New_Jersey "Camden, New Jersey"), to the site of the RCA antenna engineering facility in [Gibbsboro, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibbsboro,_New_Jersey "Gibbsboro, New Jersey"). On October 3, 1985, RCA announced it was closing the Broadcast Systems Division.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-55) In the years that followed, the broadcast product lines developed in Camden were terminated or sold off, and most of the old RCA Victor buildings and factories in Camden were demolished, except for a few of the original Victor buildings that had been declared national historic buildings.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-56) For several years, RCA spinoff [L-3 Communications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L-3_Communications "L-3 Communications") Systems East was headquartered in the famous [Nipper Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nipper_Building "Nipper Building"), but has since moved to an adjacent building built by the city for them. The renovated Nipper Building now houses shops and luxury loft apartments.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-57) Also in 1985, RCA sold the Hertz car rental company to [UAL, Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UAL_Corporation "UAL Corporation")[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-58)

## Re-acquisition and breakup by General Electric

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=RCA_Corporation&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Re-acquisition and breakup by General Electric")]

In December 1985, it was announced that General Electric would reacquire its former subsidiary for $6.28 billion in cash, or $66.50 per share of stock.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-59) GE's acquisition of RCA was the largest non-oil company merger in history up to that time and was completed on June 9, 1986. Despite initial assurances that the combined forces of GE and RCA would create a technology, manufacturing and entertainment behemoth, over the next few years, GE proceeded to sell off most of RCA's assets. It was revealed that GE's main motivation for purchasing RCA was to acquire the [NBC Television Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC_Television_Network "NBC Television Network") and the corporation's defense related businesses. In 1987, GE disposed of its 50% interest in RCA Records to its German partner [Bertelsmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertelsmann "Bertelsmann") and RCA Records became a division of [Bertelsmann Music Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertelsmann_Music_Group "Bertelsmann Music Group"); the [NBC Radio Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC_Radio_Network "NBC Radio Network") was sold to [Westwood One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westwood_One_(1976-2011) "Westwood One (1976-2011)"); RCA Global Communications Inc., a division with roots dating back to RCA's founding in 1919, was acquired by the [MCI Communications Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MCI_Communications_Corporation "MCI Communications Corporation").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-60)

In 1988, the rights to manufacture consumer electronics products under the RCA and GE brands was acquired by [Thomson Consumer Electronics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomson_Consumer_Electronics "Thomson Consumer Electronics"), in exchange for some of Thomson's medical businesses. Also in 1988, its semiconductor business (including the former RCA Solid State unit and [Intersil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intersil "Intersil")) was bought by [Harris Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harris_Corporation "Harris Corporation").[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-61) That same year, the iconic [RCA Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Building "RCA Building"), known as "30 Rock" at [Rockefeller Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockefeller_Center "Rockefeller Center") was renamed the GE Building.

In 1991, GE sold its share in RCA/Columbia to Sony Pictures which renamed the unit "Columbia TriStar Home Video" (later further renamed to Columbia TriStar Home Entertainment, now Sony Pictures Home Entertainment).[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-62)

Sarnoff Labs was put on a five-year plan whereby GE would fund all the labs' activities for the first year, then reduce its support to near zero after the fifth year. This required Sarnoff Labs to change its business model to become an industrial contract research facility. In 1988, it was transferred to [SRI International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SRI_International "SRI International") (SRI) as the [David Sarnoff Research Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Sarnoff_Research_Center "David Sarnoff Research Center"), and subsequently renamed the [Sarnoff Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarnoff_Corporation "Sarnoff Corporation"). In January 2011, Sarnoff Corporation was fully integrated into SRI.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-Sarnoff_integration-63)

In 2011, GE sold its controlling interest in [NBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC "NBC"), by this time part of the multimedia [NBCUniversal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBCUniversal "NBCUniversal") venture that included TV and cable, to [Comcast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comcast "Comcast"), and in 2013, Comcast acquired the remaining interest.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-64) After the sale of NBCUniversal, the only former RCA unit which GE retained was Government Services.

In 2022, Thomson's successor company, [Technicolor SA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technicolor_SA "Technicolor SA"), sold the [RCA trademarks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_(trademark) "RCA (trademark)")[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-65) to licensing firm Talisman Brands, Inc.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-66)[d/b/a](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D/b/a "D/b/a") Established Incorporated, stylized as _established._[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-67)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=RCA_Corporation&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Legacy")]

[![Image 33](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/88/RCA_Nipper_Camden_NJ_A.JPG/250px-RCA_Nipper_Camden_NJ_A.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:RCA_Nipper_Camden_NJ_A.JPG)

The historic [RCA Victor Building 17](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nipper_Building "Nipper Building") is one of a few remaining buildings in [Camden, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camden,_New_Jersey "Camden, New Jersey"), of the dozens that formerly housed the vast [Victor Talking Machine Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Talking_Machine_Company "Victor Talking Machine Company")/[RCA Victor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Victor "RCA Victor") manufacturing complex.

RCA [antique radios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antique_radio "Antique radio"), and early color television receivers such as the RCA Merrill/CT-100, are among the more sought-after collectible radios and televisions, due to their popularity during the [golden age of radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_age_of_radio "Golden age of radio") and the historic significance of the RCA name, as well as their styling, manufacturing quality and engineering innovations. Most collectable are the pre-war television sets manufactured by RCA beginning in 1939, including the TRK-5, TRK-9 and TRK-12 models.

The RCA Heritage Museum was established at [Rowan University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rowan_University "Rowan University") in 2012.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-68)

The historic RCA Victor Building 17, the "[Nipper Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nipper_Building "Nipper Building")", in [Camden, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camden,_New_Jersey "Camden, New Jersey"), was converted to luxury apartments in 2003.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-69)

A type of plug/jack combination used in audio and video cables is still called the [RCA connector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_connector "RCA connector").

To this day, a variety of consumer electronics including 2-in-1 tablets, televisions and telephones, home appliances and more are sold under the [RCA brand name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_(trademark) "RCA (trademark)").

[RCA Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Records "RCA Records") continues as a flagship label of [Sony Music Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Music_Entertainment "Sony Music Entertainment").

### Environmental issues

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=RCA_Corporation&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Environmental issues")]

Numerous former RCA manufacturing sites have been reported to be polluted with industrial waste.

*   A former RCA facility in Taiwan's northern county of [Taoyuan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taoyuan_City "Taoyuan City") (now Taoyuan City) polluted groundwater with toxic chemicals and led to a high incidence of cancer among former employees.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-70)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-71) The area was declared a toxic site by the [Taiwanese Environmental Protection Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_Protection_Administration_(Republic_of_China) "Environmental Protection Administration (Republic of China)"). GE and Thomson spent millions of dollars for cleanup, removing 10,000 cubic yards (7,600 m 3) of soil and installing municipal water treatment facilities for neighboring communities. A spokesman for RCA's current owners denied responsibility, saying a study conducted by the Taiwan government showed no correlation between the illnesses and the company's facilities, which shut down in 1991.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-72) On April 17, 2015, RCA lost the case and the Taipei District Court ordered RCA's current owners to compensate its former employees with a total of NT$560 million (approximately US$18.1 million).[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-73)
*   A plant in [Lancaster, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster,_Pennsylvania "Lancaster, Pennsylvania"), which RCA operated from the late 1940s to June 1986, released more than 250,000 pounds of [1,1,1-trichloroethane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1,1,1-trichloroethane "1,1,1-trichloroethane") pollutants per year from its exhaust stacks. Tests by the [United States Environmental Protection Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Environmental_Protection_Agency "United States Environmental Protection Agency") (EPA) in the late 1980s and early 1990s, found the groundwater contaminated by [trichloroethylene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichloroethylene "Trichloroethylene") (TCE) and [1,2-dichloroethylene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1,2-dichloroethylene "1,2-dichloroethylene") (1,2-DCE).[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-epa.gov-74) In 1991 and 1992, contaminants were detected in monitoring wells on the east side of the [Conestoga River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conestoga_River "Conestoga River") in Lancaster. EPA designated [General Electric Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Electric "General Electric") to clean up the area.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-epa.gov_ge_lancaster_pa-75)
*   The shallow and deep groundwater aquifers beneath the [Intersil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intersil "Intersil") Facility in [Mountaintop, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountaintop,_Pennsylvania "Mountaintop, Pennsylvania"), which RCA operated in the 1960s and later sold to [Harris Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harris_Corporation "Harris Corporation"), were found in 1999 to contain elevated levels of [volatile organic compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volatile_organic_compound "Volatile organic compound").[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-76)
*   A site in [Burlington, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_Massachusetts "Burlington, Massachusetts"), which RCA used from 1958 to 1994 to make and test military electronics equipment, generated [hazardous waste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazardous_waste "Hazardous waste") ([VOCs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VOCs "VOCs"), [TCE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichloroethylene "Trichloroethylene"), [toluene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toluene "Toluene"), [ethylbenzene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethylbenzene "Ethylbenzene"), and [xylenes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xylene "Xylene")).[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-77)
*   In [Barceloneta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barceloneta,_Puerto_Rico "Barceloneta, Puerto Rico"), Puerto Rico, an RCA-operated plant generated wastes containing [chromium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium "Chromium"), [selenium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selenium "Selenium") and iron. Four lagoons holding chemical waste drained into the limestone [aquifer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquifer "Aquifer").[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-78)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-79) Used water from the manufacturing process (process water), containing [ferric chloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferric_chloride "Ferric chloride"), was treated onsite to remove contaminants and then was discharged into a sinkhole at the site. The treatment of process water created a [sludge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sludge "Sludge") that was stored onsite in drying beds and in surface impoundments.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-80)

We are constantly working to enhance the user experience for both contributors and readers, improve site security, and ensure reliable access to our websites globally. This infrastructure and product support sustain one of the top ten most visited websites in the world, all at a fraction of the cost of popular for-profit websites.

32% Support for Volunteers

**RCA Corporation**, founded as the **Radio Corporation of America**, was a major American [electronics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronics_industry "Electronics industry") company in existence from 1919 to 1987. Initially, RCA was a [patent trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patent_pool "Patent pool") owned by a partnership of [General Electric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Electric "General Electric") (GE), [Westinghouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westinghouse_Electric_Corporation "Westinghouse Electric Corporation"), [AT&T Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AT&T_Corporation "AT&T Corporation") and [United Fruit Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Fruit_Company "United Fruit Company"). It became an independent company in 1932 after the partners agreed to divest their ownerships in settling an [antitrust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_antitrust_law "United States antitrust law") lawsuit by the United States.

An innovative and progressive company, RCA was the dominant electronics and communications firm in the United States for over five decades. In the early 1920s, RCA was at the forefront of the mushrooming radio industry, both as a major manufacturer of [radio receivers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_receiver "Radio receiver") and as the exclusive manufacturer of the first [superheterodyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superheterodyne "Superheterodyne") receiver. In 1926, the company founded the [National Broadcasting Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Broadcasting_Company "National Broadcasting Company") (NBC), the first nationwide radio network. During the 1920s and 1930s RCA also pioneered the introduction and development of broadcast television—both black and white and especially [color television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television "Color television"). Throughout most of its existence, RCA was closely identified with the leadership of [David Sarnoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Sarnoff "David Sarnoff"). He became general manager at the company's founding, served as president from 1930 to 1965, and remained active as chairman of the board until the end of 1969.

Until the 1970s, RCA maintained a seemingly impregnable stature as corporate America's leading name in technology, innovation, and home entertainment. However, the company's performance began to weaken as it expanded beyond its original focus—developing and marketing consumer electronics and communications in the US—towards the larger goal of operating as a diversified multinational conglomerate. The company also faced increasing domestic competition from international electronics firms such as [Sony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony "Sony"), [Philips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philips "Philips"), [Matsushita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panasonic "Panasonic") and [Mitsubishi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitsubishi "Mitsubishi"). RCA suffered enormous financial losses attempting to enter the mainframe computer industry, and in other failed projects including the [CED videodisc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CED_videodisc "CED videodisc") system.

By the mid 1980s, RCA was rebounding but the company was never able to regain its former eminence. In 1986, RCA was reacquired by General Electric during the [Jack Welch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Welch "Jack Welch") era at GE. Welch sold or liquidated most of RCA's assets, retaining only [NBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC "NBC") and some government services units. Today, RCA exists as a [brand name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brand_name "Brand name") only; the various [RCA trademarks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_(trademark) "RCA (trademark)") are currently owned by [Sony Music Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Music_Entertainment "Sony Music Entertainment") and [Vantiva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vantiva "Vantiva"), which in turn license the RCA brand name and trademarks for various products to several other companies, including [Voxx International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voxx_International "Voxx International"), Curtis International, AVC Multimedia, [TCL Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TCL_Corporation "TCL Corporation"), and Express LUCK International.

## Establishment by General Electric

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=RCA_Corporation&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Establishment by General Electric")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/1921_Radio_Corporation_of_America_%28Worldwide_Wireless%29_logo.jpg/250px-1921_Radio_Corporation_of_America_%28Worldwide_Wireless%29_logo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1921_Radio_Corporation_of_America_(Worldwide_Wireless)_logo.jpg)

Company logo in 1921 stressed its leadership in international communication.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-3)

RCA originated as a reorganization of the [Marconi Wireless Telegraph Company of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marconi_Wireless_Telegraph_Company_of_America "Marconi Wireless Telegraph Company of America"), commonly called "American Marconi". In 1897, the Wireless Telegraph and Signal Company, Limited, was founded in London to promote the radio—then known as "wireless telegraphy"—inventions of [Guglielmo Marconi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guglielmo_Marconi "Guglielmo Marconi"). As part of worldwide expansion, American Marconi was organized as a subsidiary in 1899, holding the rights to Marconi patents in the United States and Cuba.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-4) In 1912, American Marconi took control of the assets of the bankrupt [United Wireless Telegraph Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Wireless_Telegraph_Company "United Wireless Telegraph Company"), and from that point forward, was the dominant radio communications company in the United States.

When the United States entered [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") in April 1917, the federal government took control of most civilian radio stations to use them for the war effort. Although the government planned to restore civilian ownership of the radio stations once the war ended, many [United States Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy") officials hoped to retain a monopoly on radio communication even after the war. Contrary to instructions it had received, the Navy began purchasing large numbers of radio stations. When the war ended, Congress rejected the Navy's efforts to have peacetime control of the radio industry and instructed that the Navy return the stations to the original owners.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-5)

Due to national security considerations, the Navy was particularly concerned about returning high-powered international stations to American Marconi, since the majority of its stock was in foreign hands, and the British already largely controlled the international undersea telegraph cables. This concern was increased by the announcement in late 1918 of the formation of the Pan-American Wireless Telegraph and Telephone Company,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-6) a joint venture between American Marconi and the [Federal Telegraph Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Telegraph_Company "Federal Telegraph Company"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-7) with plans to set up service between the United States and South America.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-8)

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f6/200-kw_HF_Alternator.jpg/250px-200-kw_HF_Alternator.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:200-kw_HF_Alternator.jpg)

Alexanderson 200-kW motor alternator transmitter installed at the U.S. Navy's New Brunswick, New Jersey station[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-9)

The Navy had installed a high-powered [Alexanderson alternator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexanderson_alternator "Alexanderson alternator"), built by General Electric (GE), at the American Marconi transmitter site in New Brunswick, New Jersey. It proved to be superior for transatlantic transmissions to the [spark-gap transmitters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spark-gap_transmitter "Spark-gap transmitter") that had been traditionally used by the Marconi companies. Marconi officials were so impressed by the capabilities of the Alexanderson alternators that they began making preparations to adopt them as their standard transmitters for international communication. A tentative plan made with General Electric proposed that over a two-year period the Marconi companies would purchase most of GE's alternator production. However, the U.S. Navy objected to the plan, fearing British domination in international radio communications and the national security concerns this raised.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-formation-10)

The Navy, claiming support from U.S. President [Woodrow Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodrow_Wilson "Woodrow Wilson"), looked for an alternative that would result in an "all-American" company taking over the American Marconi assets. In April 1919, two naval officers, [Admiral H. G. Bullard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_H._G._Bullard "William H. G. Bullard") and [Commander S. C. Hooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Caldwell_Hooper "Stanford Caldwell Hooper"), met with GE president [Owen D. Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_D._Young "Owen D. Young"), and requested a suspension of the pending alternator sales to the Marconi companies. This would leave General Electric without a buyer for its transmitters, so the officers proposed that GE purchase American Marconi, and use the assets to form its own radio communications subsidiary. Young consented to this proposal, which, effective November 20, 1919, transformed American Marconi into the Radio Corporation of America. The decision to form the new company was promoted as a patriotic gesture. The corporate officers were required to be citizens of the United States, with a majority of the company stock to be held by U.S. citizens.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-formation-10)

Upon its founding, RCA was the largest radio communications firm in the United States.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-11) Most of the former American Marconi staff continued to work for RCA. Owen Young became the chairman of the board of the new company. Former American Marconi vice president and general manager E. J. Nally become RCA's first president. Nally was succeeded by Major General [James G. Harbord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_G._Harbord "James G. Harbord"), who served from 1922 until January 3, 1930, when Harbord replaced Owen Young as chairman of the board. David Sarnoff, who was RCA's founding general manager, became its third president on the same day. RCA worked closely with the federal government and felt it deserved to maintain its predominant role in U.S. radio communications. At the company's recommendation, President Wilson appointed Rear Admiral Bullard "to attend the stockholders' and director's meetings... in order that he may present and discuss informally the Government's views and interests".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-12)

The radio industry had been making technical advances, particularly in the area of vacuum tube technology and GE needed access to additional patents before its new subsidiary could be fully competitive. During this time American Marconi had been steadily falling behind others in the industry. The two companies then proceeded to negotiate a series of mutually beneficial cross-licensing agreements between themselves and various other companies in the industry. On July 1, 1920, the [American Telephone & Telegraph Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Telephone_&_Telegraph_Company "American Telephone & Telegraph Company") (AT&T), agreed to purchase 500,000 shares of RCA—although it divested these shares in early 1923. The [United Fruit Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Fruit_Company "United Fruit Company") held a small portfolio of radio patents,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-13) and signed two agreements in 1921. GE's traditional electric company rival, the [Westinghouse Electric & Manufacturing Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westinghouse_Electric_Corporation "Westinghouse Electric Corporation"), had also purchased rights to some critical patents, including one for heterodyne receiving originally issued to [Reginald Fessenden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reginald_Fessenden "Reginald Fessenden"), plus [regenerative circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regenerative_circuit "Regenerative circuit") and [superheterodyne receiver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superheterodyne_receiver "Superheterodyne receiver") patents issued to [Edwin Armstrong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Armstrong "Edwin Armstrong"). Westinghouse used this position to negotiate a cross-licensing agreement, effective July 1, 1921, that included a concession that 40% of RCA's equipment purchases would be from Westinghouse. Following these transactions, GE owned 30.1% of RCA's stock, Westinghouse 20.6%, AT&T 10.3%, and United Fruit 4.1%, with the remaining 34.9% owned by individual shareholders.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-14)

In 1930, RCA agreed to occupy the yet-to-be-constructed landmark skyscraper of the [Rockefeller Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockefeller_Center "Rockefeller Center") complex, [30 Rockefeller Plaza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/30_Rockefeller_Plaza "30 Rockefeller Plaza"), which in 1933 became known as the RCA Building (renamed the GE Building in 1988 and currently known as the Comcast Building after [Comcast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comcast "Comcast") acquired NBC). This lease was critical for enabling the massive project to proceed as a commercially viable venture—David Rockefeller cited RCA's action as being responsible for "the salvation of the project".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-15)

## Radio development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=RCA_Corporation&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Radio development")]

### International and marine communication

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=RCA_Corporation&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: International and marine communication")]

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c2/Proposed_RCA_Radio_Central_facility_at_Rocky_Point%2C_Long_Island%2C_New_York.jpg/250px-Proposed_RCA_Radio_Central_facility_at_Rocky_Point%2C_Long_Island%2C_New_York.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Proposed_RCA_Radio_Central_facility_at_Rocky_Point,_Long_Island,_New_York.jpg)

Illustration of how a fully built RCA Radio Central facility at [Rocky Point, Long Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_Point,_Long_Island "Rocky Point, Long Island"), New York would have appeared. Only two of the twelve "antenna spokes" were actually built.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-16)

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/STS-61-C_SATCOM_Ku-1_deployment.jpg/250px-STS-61-C_SATCOM_Ku-1_deployment.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-61-C_SATCOM_Ku-1_deployment.jpg)

RCA [Satcom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satcom_(satellite) "Satcom (satellite)") K1 geostationary communications satellite deployed from [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle")[_Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") in 1986

RCA's primary business objectives at its founding were to provide equipment and services for seagoing vessels, and "worldwide wireless" communication in competition with existing international undersea telegraph cables. To provide the international service, the company soon undertook a massive project to build a "Radio Central" communications hub at [Rocky Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_Point,_New_York "Rocky Point, New York"), [Long Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island "Long Island"), New York, designed to achieve "the realization of the vision of communication engineers to transmit messages to all points of the world from a single centrally located source". Construction began in July 1920, and the site was dedicated on November 5, 1921, after two of the proposed twelve antenna spokes had been completed, and two of the 200-kilowatt alternators installed. The debut transmissions received replies from stations in 17 countries.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-17)

Although the initial installation would remain in operation, the additional antenna spokes and alternator installations would not be completed, due to a major discovery about radio signal propagation. While investigating transmitter "harmonics" – unwanted additional radio signals produced at higher frequencies than a station's normal transmission frequency – Westinghouse's [Frank Conrad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Conrad "Frank Conrad") unexpectedly found that in some cases the harmonics could be heard farther than the primary signal, something previously thought impossible, as high-frequency [shortwave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shortwave "Shortwave") signals, which had poor groundwave coverage, were thought to have a very limited transmission range. In 1924, Conrad demonstrated to Sarnoff that a low-powered shortwave station in East Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania could be readily received in London by a simple receiver using a curtain rod as an antenna, matching, at a small fraction of the cost, the performance of the massive alternator transmitters. In 1926, [Harold H. Beverage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_H._Beverage "Harold H. Beverage") further reported that a shortwave signal, transmitted on a 15-meter wavelength (approximately 20 MHz), was received in South America more readily during the daytime than the 200-kilowatt alternator transmissions.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-18)

The Alexanderson alternators, control of which had led to RCA's formation, were now considered obsolete, and international radio communication would be primarily conducted using [vacuum tube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacuum_tube "Vacuum tube") transmitters operating on shortwave bands. RCA would continue to operate international telecommunications services for the remainder of its existence, through its subsidiary RCA Communications, Inc., and later the RCA Global Communications Company. In 1975, the company formed [RCA American Communications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_American_Communications "RCA American Communications"), which operated its Satcom series of [geostationary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geostationary_orbit "Geostationary orbit")[communications satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_satellite "Communications satellite"). International shortwave links were in turn largely supplanted by communications satellites, especially for distributing network radio and television programming.

At the time RCA was founded in 1919, all radio and telegraphic communication between China and the US, including official messages, were sent through either German radio or British cable links. The U.S. Navy lobbied RCA to seek a [concession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concession_(contract) "Concession (contract)") for a radio link to China, however the company was reluctant because its other concessions were already operating at a loss. This link began operation in 1928. The [Mackay Radio and Telegraph Company of California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mackay_Radio "Mackay Radio") signed a similar agreement with China in 1932. RCA claimed this was [breach of contract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breach_of_contract "Breach of contract") on the grounds that its 1928 agreement had given it exclusive rights. The dispute went to arbitration, and in 1935 a decision, issued in _[Radio Corporation of America v China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio\_Corporation\_of\_America\_v\_China "Radio Corporation of America v China")_, concluded the Mackay concession was valid, because the earlier RCA concession had not granted exclusive rights.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-19)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation#cite_note-20)

#### Patents and licensing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=RCA_Corporation&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Patents and licensing")]

Main article: [Patents and licensing in early radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patents_and_licensing_in_early_radio "Patents and licensing in early radio")

The formation of RCA was closely tied to the control and licensing of key wireless patents. Agreements among General Electric, Westinghouse, AT&T, and RCA created a large patent pool covering many radio technologies, including vacuum tubes and receiver circuits. These arrangements influenced which companies could manufacture radio equipment and played an important role in shaping the early radio industry.
