From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

"The Torture Report" redirects here. For the film also known as The Torture Report, see [The Report (2019 film)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Report_(2019_film) "The Report (2019 film)").

Report of the United States government

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/US_Senate_Report_on_CIA_Detention_Interrogation_Program.pdf/page1-250px-US_Senate_Report_on_CIA_Detention_Interrogation_Program.pdf.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:US_Senate_Report_on_CIA_Detention_Interrogation_Program.pdf)

The U.S. Senate Report on CIA Detention Interrogation Program that details the use of torture during CIA detention and interrogation.

The **Committee Study of the Central Intelligence Agency's Detention and Interrogation Program**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1) is a report compiled by the bipartisan [United States Senate Select Committee on Intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Select_Committee_on_Intelligence "United States Senate Select Committee on Intelligence") (SSCI) about the [Central Intelligence Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Intelligence_Agency "Central Intelligence Agency") (CIA)'s Detention and Interrogation Program and its use of torture during interrogation on detainees in CIA custody. The report covers CIA activities before, during, and after the "[war on terror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_on_terror "War on terror")". The initial report was approved on December 13, 2012, by a vote of 9–6, with seven [Democrats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democrat_(United_States) "Democrat (United States)"), one independent, and one Republican voting in favor of the report and six Republicans voting in opposition.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-LA_Timeline-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Opposition_Response-3)

The more than 6,700-page report (including 38,000 footnotes)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-feinsteinsenate-4) details the history of the CIA's Detention and Interrogation Program and the Committee's 20 findings and conclusions. On December 9, 2014, the SSCI released a 525-page portion that consisted of key findings and an executive summary of the full report. It took more than five years to complete.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-GuardDec0914-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-feinstein40-6) The full unredacted report remains classified.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-NPR-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-GuardDec0814-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-9)

The report details actions by CIA officials including torturing prisoners, providing misleading or false information about classified CIA programs to the president, Department of Justice, Congress, and the media, impeding government oversight and internal criticism, and mismanaging the program. It also revealed the existence of previously unknown detainees, that more detainees were subjected to "[enhanced interrogation techniques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enhanced_interrogation_techniques "Enhanced interrogation techniques")" (widely understood to be a euphemism for [torture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torture "Torture")) than was previously disclosed, and that more techniques were used without Department of Justice approval. It concluded that the use of enhanced interrogation techniques did not yield unique intelligence that saved lives (as the CIA claimed), nor was it useful in gaining cooperation from detainees, and that the program damaged the United States' international standing.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1)

Some people, including some CIA officials and U.S. [Republicans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)"), disputed the report's conclusions and said it provided an incomplete picture of the program. Others criticized the publishing of the report, citing its potential for damage to the U.S. and the contentious history of its development. Former Republican presidential nominee [John McCain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCain "John McCain") praised the release of the report. Upon the report's release, then-president [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") stated, "One of the strengths that makes America exceptional is our willingness to openly confront our past, face our imperfections, make changes and do better."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-10)

In the wake of the release of the report's executive summary, a large number of individuals and organizations called for the prosecution of the CIA and government officials who perpetrated, approved, or provided legal cover for the torture of detainees;[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-HRW_Roadmap-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Bloomberg2-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-BBC-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Torture_Fight_Set_Back_by_U.S._Failure_to_Prosecute,_U.N._Official_Says-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-NYT_Editorial_Board-15) however, prosecutions are considered unlikely.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-16) The U.S. has also passed legislation, sponsored by Senators McCain and [Dianne Feinstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dianne_Feinstein "Dianne Feinstein"), to prevent U.S. agencies from using many of the torture techniques described in the report.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-hr1735-17)

The 2019 film _[The Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Report\_(2019\_film) "The Report (2019 film)")_ covers the decade-long time period that led to the final creation and publication of the report.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-PBS_The_Report_20191129-18)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Impetus for the report

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Impetus for the report")]

See also: [2005 CIA interrogation tapes destruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_CIA_interrogation_tapes_destruction "2005 CIA interrogation tapes destruction")

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/Dianne_Feinstein%2C_official_Senate_photo_2.jpg/250px-Dianne_Feinstein%2C_official_Senate_photo_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dianne_Feinstein,_official_Senate_photo_2.jpg)

Senator [Dianne Feinstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dianne_Feinstein "Dianne Feinstein") (D-CA) was the chair of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence from 2009 to early 2015

California Senator [Dianne Feinstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dianne_Feinstein "Dianne Feinstein") said that the initial investigation began after press reports emerged stating that in 2005, CIA [Director of the National Clandestine Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director_of_the_National_Clandestine_Service "Director of the National Clandestine Service")[Jose Rodriguez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_Rodriguez_(intelligence_officer) "Jose Rodriguez (intelligence officer)") destroyed almost 100 video recordings of interrogations over objections from CIA and White House legal staff. The tapes showed CIA officers and contractors using torture techniques such as waterboarding on detainees [Abu Zubaydah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Zubaydah "Abu Zubaydah") and [Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_al-Rahim_al-Nashiri "Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri"). The CIA did not inform the [United States Senate Select Committee on Intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Select_Committee_on_Intelligence "United States Senate Select Committee on Intelligence") (SSCI) that Rodriguez had destroyed the tapes, and the committee had not known they had existed. SSCI believed that Rodriguez was covering up illegal activities by the CIA, although the committee had initially been told by CIA officials that Rodriguez was not engaging in "destruction of evidence".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-GuardDec0814-8) Rodriguez preemptively criticized the report in an [op-ed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Op-ed "Op-ed") for _[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Washington\_Post "The Washington Post")_ on December 5, 2014.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-WaPoDec5-19) In addition to destroying the torture tapes, the Committee's report shows that Rodriguez was heavily involved in the CIA's use of torture, including overseeing [black sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_site "Black site") where torture took place,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):57 of 499 preventing CIA [Counterterrorism Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterterrorism_Center "Counterterrorism Center") (CTC) legal staff from implementing vetting processes for interrogators,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):59 of 499 provided misleading information to the [Department of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") about a detainee's identity,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):120 of 499 and participated in the payment of millions of dollars to a country hosting a black site.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):140 of 499

CIA Director [Michael Hayden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Hayden_(general) "Michael Hayden (general)") told the Committee on December 11, 2007, that if the Committee had asked for the videos, the CIA would have provided them, and offered the Committee written summaries of the interrogation sessions depicted on the destroyed tapes. CIA records show that the decision to destroy the tapes came shortly after CIA attorneys raised concerns about Congress discovering the tapes' existence.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-feinsteinsenate-4)

[Jane Mayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Mayer "Jane Mayer")'s book _[The Dark Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Dark\_Side\_(book) "The Dark Side (book)")_ stated that the CIA also neglected to inform the [9/11 Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9/11_Commission "9/11 Commission") that these tapes existed: "In a meeting on December 23, 2003, [Commission executive director Philip D.] Zelikow demanded that the CIA at the very least provide any and all documents responsive to its requests, even if the Commission had not specifically asked for them. [CIA Director George] Tenet replied by alluding to several documents he thought would be helpful. But in an omission that would later become part of a criminal investigation, neither Tenet nor anyone else from the CIA in the meeting mentioned that, in fact, the Agency had in its possession at that point hundreds of hours of videotapes of the interrogations of Abu Zubayda and Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri, both of whom were waterboarded."[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-janemeyer-20):279

In December 2007, the committee opened an investigation into the tape destruction and designated four staffers to conduct the investigation, which they completed around early 2009.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-feinsteinsenate-4)

### Development of the report

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Development of the report")]

On February 11, 2009, the committee began considering a broader review of the CIA's detention and interrogation practices after committee staff presented a summary of the operational cables detailing the interrogations of [Abu Zubaydah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Zubaydah "Abu Zubaydah") and [Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_al-Rahim_al-Nashiri "Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-LA_Timeline-2) On March 5, 2009, the Senate Intelligence Committee voted 14–1 to open an investigation into the CIA detention and interrogation program.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-LA_Timeline-2) In August 2009, [Attorney General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Attorney_General "United States Attorney General")[Eric Holder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Holder "Eric Holder") announced a parallel preliminary criminal investigation into the use of unauthorized interrogation techniques by CIA officials.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-LA_Timeline-2) As a result of the attorney general's investigation, the [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_(United_States) "Republican (United States)") minority on the SSCI concluded that many witnesses were unlikely to participate in the investigation for fear of criminal liability.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Opposition_Response-3) Citing the attorney general investigation as their reason, the Republican minority of the SSCI withdrew their participation from the investigation in September 2009.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-LA_Timeline-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Opposition_Response-3)

The Senate investigation was led by Committee staffer and former FBI investigator [Daniel J. Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_J._Jones "Daniel J. Jones"), and was prepared following a review of more than 6.3 million pages of documents, cables, emails, and other materials principally provided by the CIA.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-HuffPost-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-CNNCost-22) The document production phase lasted more than three years and was completed in July 2012.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-intelligence-23) As described in the Senate report, an additional 9,400 classified documents repeatedly requested by the SSCI were withheld by the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House") under a claim of [executive privilege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_privilege "Executive privilege").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Opposition_Response-3)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-HuffPost-21)

Despite the initial expectation that interviews would be used, no formal interviews or hearings were conducted in the preparation of the report.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Opposition_Response-3)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-SusanCollinsStatement-24) The lack of interviews and hearings was one of the chief complaints of the Republican minority on SSCI.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Opposition_Response-3) However, the report included CIA officials' on-the-record statements in classified committee hearings, written statements, and interviews conducted through the CIA Inspector General's office and the Agency's oral history program, as well as through the formal response to the committee in June 2013 after reading the report. These statements and interviews included those from CIA director [George Tenet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Tenet "George Tenet"), CTC director [Jose Rodriguez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_Rodriguez_(intelligence_officer) "Jose Rodriguez (intelligence officer)"), CIA general counsel Scott Muller, CIA deputy director of operations [James Pavitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Pavitt "James Pavitt"), CIA acting general counsel [John Rizzo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Rizzo "John Rizzo"), CIA deputy director [John McLaughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_E._McLaughlin "John E. McLaughlin"), and a variety of interrogators, lawyers, medical personnel, senior counterterrorism analysts and managers of the detention and interrogation program.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-interrogation-25)

The CIA estimated that approximately $40 million in personnel time and resources was spent assisting the investigation, but this was largely because of the CIA's insistence on hiring Centra Technology contractors to review documents prior to presenting them to the Committee and establishing a separate secure facility and computer network for CIA and Committee staff to use during the review.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-CNNCost-22)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-contractor-26) This deviated from the standard document-sharing process, in which the CIA provides documents for Committee staff to review in Committee offices.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-feinstein40-6)

The final report was approved on December 13, 2012, by a vote of 9–6, with eight [Democrats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democrat_(United_States) "Democrat (United States)") and one Republican ([Olympia Snowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympia_Snowe "Olympia Snowe")) voting in favor of publication and six Republicans voting in opposition, and the published minority views of Senator [Chambliss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxby_Chambliss "Saxby Chambliss") were joined by Senators [Burr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Burr "Richard Burr"), [Risch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Risch "Jim Risch"), [Coats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Coats "Dan Coats"), [Rubio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Rubio "Marco Rubio"), and [Coburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Coburn "Tom Coburn").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-LA_Timeline-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Opposition_Response-3)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-27) Republican Senator [John McCain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCain "John McCain"), a member of the Committee ex officio, did not have a vote, but he supported approval alongside Snowe.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-28) On April 3, 2014, the SSCI voted 11–3 to submit a revised version of the executive summary, findings, and recommendations of the report for declassification analysis in preparation for future public release.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-LA_Timeline-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Opposition_Response-3) Independent Senator [Angus King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angus_King "Angus King") and Republican Senator [Susan Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Collins "Susan Collins") supported the release of the report.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-29) After eight months, involving contentious negotiations about what details should remain classified,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-NPR-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-GuardDec0814-8) the revised executive summary, findings, and recommendations were made public with many [redactions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanitization_(classified_information) "Sanitization (classified information)") on December 9, 2014.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-LA_Timeline-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Opposition_Response-3)

The CIA had demanded that the Committee redact the names of all detainees, all CIA officer's pseudonyms, and the names of all countries that hosted black sites. Daniel J. Jones told _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_ that the Agency wanted to redact other material, such as references to [Allah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allah "Allah"). The CIA wanted pseudonyms to be used for contractors and interrogators [James Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Elmer_Mitchell "James Elmer Mitchell") and [Bruce Jessen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Jessen "Bruce Jessen"), despite the fact that they had both been identified publicly prior to the report's release.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-crisis-30) The report ended up including detainee names, and used pseudonyms (such as "CIA OFFICER 1") for several Agency officers, but redacted the names of almost all others, as well as black site host countries.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-charmed-31)

Information about the cooperation of foreign agencies with the CIA has been redacted from the report. The British chairman of the [Intelligence and Security Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelligence_and_Security_Committee "Intelligence and Security Committee") stated they would request access to anything taken out of the report at the request of British agencies.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-33)

#### Panetta Review and CIA hacking incident

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Panetta Review and CIA hacking incident")]

See also: [Panetta Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panetta_Review "Panetta Review")

On December 17, 2013, Sen. [Mark Udall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Udall "Mark Udall") (D-CO) revealed the existence of a secret internal review (the "Panetta Review") conducted by the CIA that was consistent with the Senate's report but conflicted with the CIA's official response to the report.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-nytimes03072014-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-35) In January 2014, CIA officials claimed that the Intelligence Committee had accessed portions of the "Panetta Review" and removed them from CIA facilities in 2010 without CIA authorization.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-mcclatchy-36) In March 2014, Sen. [Dianne Feinstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dianne_Feinstein "Dianne Feinstein") (D-CA), chairwoman of the Intelligence Committee, confirmed that a portion of the "Panetta Review" had been copied and transferred to a safe in the Senate's [Hart Office Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hart_Office_Building "Hart Office Building"). She stated that the action was necessary to protect the documents from the CIA, [which had destroyed videotapes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_CIA_interrogation_tapes_destruction "2005 CIA interrogation tapes destruction") depicting brutal interrogation methods in 2005.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-erupts-37)

During the review process the CIA had removed hundreds of pages of documents from the Committee staff's CIA-provided computer network (called "RDINet" for "rendition, detention, and interrogation") without informing Committee staff. According to Senator Feinstein, when Committee staff inquired about the missing documents, CIA staff initially denied the files had been removed, then blamed IT contractors, and finally falsely claimed that the White House had requested their removal.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-furious-38)

When negotiating the review process, the Committee and the CIA came to an agreement that the CIA would establish "a walled-off network share-drive" accessible only to Committee staff, and that "CIA access to the walled off network shared drive will be limited to CIA information technology staff, except as authorized by the committee or its staff."[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-secrets-39)

During an "extraordinary"[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-wsj03112014-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-politico03112014-41) 45-minute speech on March 11, 2014, Feinstein said the CIA unlawfully searched the Intelligence Committee's computers to determine how the committee staff obtained the "Panetta Review" documents. Feinstein also said that the CIA's acting general counsel, later identified as [Robert Eatinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Eatinger "Robert Eatinger"), requested the FBI conduct a criminal inquiry into the committee staff who had accessed and relocated the "Panetta Review" documents. She said she believed that the request was "a potential effort to intimidate [Intelligence Committee] staff."[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-wapo03112014-43) Eatinger had been involved in the destruction of video tapes in 2005 (which started the Senate investigation),[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-erupts-37)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-44) and Feinstein added that Eatinger was mentioned by name over 1,600 times in the Committee's full report. The same day that Feinstein made the allegations, CIA director [John O. Brennan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_O._Brennan "John O. Brennan") denied that the CIA searched the Senate computers, stating, "As far as the allegations of, you know, CIA hacking into, you know, Senate computers, nothing could be further from the truth. I mean we wouldn't do that. I mean that's just beyond the – you know, the scope of reason in terms of what we would do... When the facts come out on this, I think a lot of people who are claiming that there has been this tremendous sort of spying and monitoring and hacking will be proved wrong."[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-erupts-37)

On July 31, 2014, the CIA's Inspector General confirmed that the CIA had improperly gained access to and searched the Senate Intelligence Committee's computer network, including that CIA employees had accessed the Committee's computers, read Committee staff's email, and sent a criminal referral to the Department of Justice based on false information.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-45) A Justice Department spokesman later announced that they would not be pursuing charges in the hacking incident.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-46) An internal review panel appointed by Brennan contended that the searches "were lawful and in some cases done at the behest of [John O. Brennan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_O._Brennan "John O. Brennan"), the C.I.A. director."[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Hacking_Panel-47)

## Findings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Findings")]

### Findings listed in the report

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Findings listed in the report")]

The more-than 6,700-page report produced 20 key findings. They are, verbatim from the unclassified Executive Summary report:[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1)

1.   The CIA's use of its [enhanced interrogation techniques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enhanced_interrogation_techniques "Enhanced interrogation techniques") was not an effective means of acquiring [intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelligence_assessment "Intelligence assessment") or gaining cooperation from detainees.
2.   The CIA's justification for the use of its enhanced interrogation techniques rested on inaccurate claims of their effectiveness.
3.   The interrogations of CIA detainees were brutal and far worse than the CIA represented to policymakers and others.
4.   The conditions of confinement for CIA detainees were harsher than the CIA had represented to policymakers and others.
5.   The CIA repeatedly provided inaccurate information to the [Department of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Justice "United States Department of Justice") (DOJ), impeding a proper legal analysis of the CIA's Detention and Interrogation Program.
6.   The CIA has actively avoided or impeded congressional oversight of the program.
7.   The CIA impeded effective White House oversight and decision-making.
8.   The CIA's operation and management of the program complicated, and in some cases impeded, the national security missions of other [Executive Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Executive_Branch "United States Executive Branch") agencies.
9.   The CIA impeded oversight by the CIA's [Office of Inspector General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_inspector_general_(United_States) "Office of inspector general (United States)").
10.   The CIA coordinated the release of classified information to the media, including inaccurate information concerning the effectiveness of the CIA's enhanced interrogation techniques.
11.   The CIA was unprepared as it began operating its Detention and Interrogation Program more than six months after being granted detention authorities.
12.   The CIA's management and operation of its Detention and Interrogation Program was deeply flawed throughout the program's duration, particularly so in 2002 and early 2003.
13.   Two contract psychologists devised the CIA's enhanced interrogation techniques and played a central role in the operation, assessments, and management of the CIA's Detention and Interrogation Program. By 2005, the CIA had overwhelmingly outsourced operations related to the program.
14.   CIA detainees were subjected to coercive interrogation techniques that had not been approved by the Department of Justice or had not been authorized by CIA Headquarters.
15.   The CIA did not conduct a comprehensive or accurate accounting of the number of individuals it detained, and held individuals who did not meet the legal standard for detention. The CIA's claims about the number of detainees held and subjected to its enhanced interrogation techniques were inaccurate.
16.   The CIA failed to adequately evaluate the effectiveness of its enhanced interrogation techniques.
17.   The CIA rarely reprimanded or held personnel accountable for serious or significant violations, inappropriate activities, and systematic and individual management failures.
18.   The CIA marginalized and ignored numerous internal critiques, criticisms, and objections concerning the operation and management of the CIA's Detention and Interrogation Program.
19.   The CIA's Detention and Interrogation Program was inherently unsustainable and had effectively ended by 2006 due to unauthorized press disclosures, reduced cooperation from other nations, and legal and oversight concerns.
20.   The CIA's Detention and Interrogation Program damaged the United States' standing in the world, and resulted in other significant monetary and non-monetary costs.

### Findings as reported by media outlets

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Findings as reported by media outlets")]

#### Examples of torture and abuse of prisoners

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Examples of torture and abuse of prisoners")]

*   The CIA had [force-fed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Force-feeding "Force-feeding") some prisoners [orally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mouth "Mouth") and/or [anally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rectal_feeding "Rectal feeding") in order to establish "total control over the detainee."[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-NYT.Fault-48) The report notes that CIA documents indicate "Chief of Interrogations [redacted] also ordered the rectal rehydration of KSM without a determination of medical need, a procedure that the chief of interrogations would later characterize as illustrative of the interrogator’s 'total control over the detainee.'"[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):82 of 499
*   The Committee found that "[a]t least five CIA detainees were subjected to 'rectal rehydration' or rectal feeding without documented medical necessity."[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-CIA_Report's_Most_Shocking_Passages-49) These detainees are listed as [Abu Zubaydah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Zubaydah "Abu Zubaydah"), [Khalid Shaykh Mohammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalid_Shaykh_Mohammad "Khalid Shaykh Mohammad"), [Majid Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majid_Khan_(detainee) "Majid Khan (detainee)"), and Marwan al-Jabbur.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):114 of 499
*   At least one prisoner was "diagnosed with chronic hemorrhoids, an anal fissure and symptomatic [rectal prolapse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rectal_prolapse "Rectal prolapse")," symptoms normally associated with a violent rape.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Mic.com1-50) The report identified this detainee as [Mustafa al-Hawsawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mustafa_al-Hawsawi "Mustafa al-Hawsawi").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):100 of 499
*   CIA officials, including general counsel [Scott Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Miller_(CIA)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Scott Miller (CIA) (page does not exist)") and deputy director of operations [James Pavitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Pavitt "James Pavitt"), were told that rectal exams of at least two prisoners had been conducted with "excessive force."[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Mic.com1-50) A CIA attorney was asked to follow up on these incidents, but the report states that "CIA records do not indicate any resolution of the inquiry."[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):100 of 499
*   CIA interrogators threatened to rape and murder children and/or family members of prisoners.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):4[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Vox1-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-svt-52) For example, according to the CIA's Inspector General, a CIA interrogator told [Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_al-Rahim_al-Nashiri "Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri") that if he did not provide information, "We could get your mother in here," and "We can bring your family in here." The interrogator also led al-Nashiri to believe that he was being held in a Middle Eastern country whose interrogators sexually abused female family members in front of detainees.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-inspectorgenreport-53):42–43
*   In November 2002 the CIA killed [Gul Rahman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gul_Rahman "Gul Rahman") during interrogation by [hypothermia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypothermia "Hypothermia").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Vox1-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-svt-52) Rahman was tortured by CIA officers and contractors and left wearing only a sweatshirt, chained to a wall in a seating position on a cold floor. No CIA employees were disciplined as a result of his death,[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Vox1-51) and the CIA officer who managed the black site where Rahman died, who was not a trained interrogator and had a history of behavioral issues,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):50 of 499 was recommended for a cash award of $2,500 for "consistently superior work" and continued to interrogate detainees.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):55 of 499
*   At least four prisoners with injuries to their legs (two with broken feet, one with a sprained ankle and one with an amputated leg) were forced to stand on their injuries.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Vox1-51) Interrogators subjected these detainees to extended periods of standing sleep deprivation without prior headquarters approval.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):101 of 499
*   Interrogators told prisoners that they would be killed. For example: one prisoner, [Abu Zubaydah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Zubaydah "Abu Zubaydah"), was told "We can never let the world know what I have done to you", another was told that the only way he would be allowed to leave the prison would be in a [coffin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffin "Coffin")-shaped confinement box.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Vox1-51)
*   One CIA interrogator who was subsequently sent home early threatened prisoner [Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_al-Rahim_al-Nashiri "Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri") with a gun and power drill, racking a handgun and revving the drill next to al-Nashiri's hooded head. The interrogator had not sought Headquarters approval for these unauthorized actions.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Mic.com1-50)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-inspectorgenreport-53):41–42
*   At least two prisoners were victims of "[mock executions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mock_execution "Mock execution")."[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Mic.com1-50) According to the CIA's Inspector General, the same debriefer who used the gun and drill on al-Nashiri claimed that he had witnessed other CIA interrogators stage an execution to scare a detainee, and several other CIA officers also said that they had witnessed or participated in mock executions.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-inspectorgenreport-53):70–72
*   Several prisoners almost died and became completely unresponsive or nearly drowned during [waterboarding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waterboarding "Waterboarding").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Vox1-51) Multiple CIA communications described CIA interrogators waterboarding Abu Zubaydah and in one session, Zubaydah "becoming completely unresponsive, with bubbles rising through his open, full mouth." He remained unresponsive until given medical attention, when he regained consciousness and expelled "copious amounts of liquid."[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):43–44 of 499
*   [Abu Zubaydah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Zubaydah "Abu Zubaydah")'s eye was so badly damaged during his time in prison that it was surgically removed.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Vox1-51)
*   The CIA [kept some prisoners awake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleep_deprivation#Interrogation "Sleep deprivation") for over one week (180 hours), as well as shorter extended periods of time. This included the use of sitting or standing stress positions that prevented sleep. Sleep deprivation caused at least five to experience "disturbing" hallucinations.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):3 of 19 of the Findings and Conclusions[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Vox1-51) The CIA claimed in its 2013 response that when detainees experienced hallucinations during sleep deprivation, medical staff intervened and allowed the detainee to sleep. However, CIA records indicate that this was not always true.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):132 of 499
*   After more than a month of torture, including loud music, dietary and temperature manipulation, sleep and sensory deprivation, and shackling, prisoner Ridha al-Najjar was psychologically traumatized to the point of being described as "a broken man."[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Vox1-51)
*   Prisoners were forced to use buckets for toilets.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Mic.com1-50) As punishment, interrogators could remove the waste bucket from a prisoner's cell.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-How_the_CIA_Lied_to_Congress_on_Torture,_According_to_Congress-54) In one case, CIA interrogators told a detainee that he could earn a bucket by cooperating, and those undergoing standing sleep deprivation were routinely put in diapers. This contradicts CIA Director Michael Hayden's assertion that "Detainees have never been denied the means – at a minimum, they've always had a bucket – to dispose of their human waste."[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):490 of 499
*   On visiting one of the CIA black sites, CIA records indicate that [Federal Bureau of Prisons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Prisons "Federal Bureau of Prisons") representatives stated "they [had] never been in a facility where individuals were so [sensory deprived](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sensory_deprivation "Sensory deprivation") i.e., constant [white noise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_noise "White noise"), no talking, everyone in the dark, with the guards wearing a light on their head when they collected and escorted a detainee to an interrogation cell, detainees constantly being shackled to the wall or floor, and the starkness of each cell (concrete and bars). There is nothing like this in the Federal Bureau of Prisons. They then explained that they understood the mission and it was their collective assessment that in spite of all this sensory deprivation, the detainees were not being treated in humanely [sic]."[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Mic.com1-50) This evaluation was of the same black site where [Gul Rahman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gul_Rahman "Gul Rahman") died after CIA interrogators beat him and left him shackled half nude on a cold floor.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):60 of 499
*   [Janat Gul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammdidullah "Hammdidullah") was tortured for months based on false accusations made by an informant known as Asset Y.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Mic.com1-50) According to CIA documents, senior CIA officers had expressed doubt about the source's credibility and Gul denied having information about imminent threats to the United States, but interrogators proceeded to subject Gul to numerous torture techniques. Even after CIA staff at the site stated that they believed Gul was not withholding information, CIA Headquarters ordered continued use of torture tactics. Gul never provided the information the CIA thought he possessed, and Asset Y admitted to fabricating the accusations against him.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):136–37 of 499
*   CIA interrogators forced detainee [Abu Zubaydah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Zubaydah "Abu Zubaydah") into a box the size of a coffin for a total of 266 hours (over 11 days) and also forced him to stay for 29 hours in a box measuring 21 inches (53 cm) wide, 2.5 feet (76 cm) deep and 2.5 feet (76 cm) high.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Bloomberg2-12) Interrogators told him that the only way he was leaving the facility was in a coffin-shaped box.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):42 of 499
*   CIA interrogators used unauthorized forms of torture, or used authorized techniques for more time or in more extreme ways than were approved, and usually faced no disciplinary action. These unauthorized techniques included forcing detainee [Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_al-Rahim_al-Nashiri "Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri") to stand with his hands shackled over his head for 2 1/2 days, racking a handgun next to his head and operating a power drill near his body.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Bloomberg2-12)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):69 of 499[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-inspectorgenreport-53):41–42[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-ciatechniques-55) Other unauthorized techniques and divergence from authorized applications of techniques included improvised stress positions,[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-inspectorgenreport-53):44[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):104 of 499 longer sleep deprivation than approved, punitive water dousing and nudity, temperature, dietary manipulation, application of the waterboard that differed from the approved methods.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-inspectorgenreport-53):5 CIA interrogators also subjected multiple detainees to unauthorized torture techniques that Headquarters later retroactively approved.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):108 of 499
*   CIA interrogators subjected one detainee, [Abu Hudhaifa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Hudhaifa "Abu Hudhaifa"), to "ice water baths" and 66 hours of standing sleep deprivation, as well as forced nudity and dietary manipulation. He was later released as the CIA had mistaken his identity.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-56) According to CIA records, Hudhaifa was one of dozens of individuals whom the CIA detained who were cases of mistaken identity or otherwise did not meet the requirements for detention.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):16 of 499
*   Torture of prisoners led to serious mental harm (e.g. [dementia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dementia "Dementia"), [paranoia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paranoia "Paranoia"), [insomnia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insomnia "Insomnia"), and attempts at [self-harm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-harm "Self-harm") [including suicide])[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-NYT.Fault-48)
*   Of the 119 known detainees, at least 39 were tortured by the CIA.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1) The report notes that this is likely a conservative estimate.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):101 of 499 The CIA also used torture on several detainees before evaluating whether they would be willing to cooperate,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Vox1-51) despite later CIA claims to the Committee that detainees were always provided the opportunity to cooperate before enhanced interrogation techniques. In 2003, CIA interrogators subjected at least six detainees to shackled nudity, sleep deprivation, or other torture techniques before any questioning took place.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):77 of 499

#### Misleading information provided by the CIA

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Misleading information provided by the CIA")]

*   The CIA's directors ([George Tenet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Tenet "George Tenet"), [Porter Goss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porter_Goss "Porter Goss") and [Michael Hayden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Hayden_(general) "Michael Hayden (general)")) provided inaccurate and misleading information to members of the [U.S. Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Congress "U.S. Congress"), the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House") and the [Director of National Intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director_of_National_Intelligence "Director of National Intelligence") about the program's effectiveness and the number of prisoners that the CIA held.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-NYT.Fault-48) For example, on December 23, 2005, Goss wrote, inaccurately, to National Security advisor [Stephen Hadley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Hadley "Stephen Hadley"), Homeland Security advisor [Frances Townsend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frances_Townsend "Frances Townsend"), and Director of National Intelligence [John Negroponte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Negroponte "John Negroponte") that the CIA's interrogation program thwarting an attack on [Heathrow Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport "Heathrow Airport") "has allowed the U.S. to save hundreds, if not thousands, of lives," and that "only 29 [detainees] have undergone interrogation that used one or more of the 13 enhanced interrogation techniques."[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):296–97 of 499
*   The CIA provided inaccurate information regarding the interrogation program to members of the media, including journalists Douglas Jehl of the _[New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_York\_Times "New York Times")_ and [Ronald Kessler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Kessler "Ronald Kessler"), as well as [Dateline NBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dateline_NBC "Dateline NBC"). This information misrepresented the interrogation program's effectiveness and the sources of specific intelligence.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-NYT.Fault-48)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):4,401–04
*   The CIA provided inaccurate information in official documents to government officials about the value of information extracted from prisoners subjected to torture (e.g. stating that information extracted from Khalid Sheikh Mohammed during torture had allowed for the capture of [Riduan Isamuddin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riduan_Isamuddin "Riduan Isamuddin"), aka Hambali).[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Vox1-51) CIA communications and records revealed that the information that led to Hambali's capture came from signals intelligence, a CIA source, and Thai authorities' investigations, not the use of enhanced interrogation techniques.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):305 of 499
*   Despite contrary statements made by the CIA's Director, Michael V. Hayden, that "all those involved in the questioning of detainees are carefully chosen and screened for demonstrated professional judgment and maturity,"[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):59 of 499 the CIA did employ individuals as interrogators who "had engaged in inappropriate detainee interrogations, had workplace anger management issues, and had reportedly admitted to sexual assault."[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Vox1-51)
*   The CIA provided false information to the Department of Justice's [Office of Legal Counsel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_Legal_Counsel "Office of Legal Counsel") about the methods of interrogation it was using against prisoners.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Bloomberg1-57)
*   CIA Deputy Director of the [National Counterterrorism Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Counterterrorism_Center "National Counterterrorism Center"), [Philip Mudd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Mudd "Philip Mudd"), discussed outreach to the media to thwart Congress, stating, "We either get out and sell, or we get hammered, which has implications beyond the media. [C]ongress reads it, cuts our authorities, mess up our budget."[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Bloomberg1-57)
*   The report found that the CIA held at least 119 detainees during the course of the interrogation program, more than the 98 previously reported to Congress.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-New_York_Times2-58)
*   An email cited in the report and prepared by a subordinate indicates that CIA Director Michael Hayden knew that the CIA had detained at least 112 detainees, but told CIA personnel to report 98, the number that had been provided to Congress. *   Several times throughout the program, CIA officers identified inaccuracies in CIA representations to other U.S. government offices and the public about the program's effectiveness. The CIA did not correct these inaccuracies, and allowed inaccurate information to remain as the CIA's official position.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):15 of 19 of the Findings and Conclusions

#### Innocent people imprisoned by the CIA

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Innocent people imprisoned by the CIA")]

At least 26 of the 119 prisoners (22%) held by the CIA were subsequently found by the CIA to have been improperly detained,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1) many having also experienced torture.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-Vox1-51)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-New_York_Times2-58) Under the memorandum of notification (MON) signed by President [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush") to establish the CIA detention program, only persons who "pose a continuing, serious threat of violence or death to U.S. persons and interests or planning terrorist activities" were eligible for detention.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1) The MON also did not reference interrogation. Two innocent people were jailed and tortured based solely on allegations from another prisoner who fabricated information after having been tortured himself.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-New_York_Times2-58) Two former [intelligence sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Informant "Informant") were jailed and tortured by accident.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):133[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-New_York_Times2-58) One [mentally challenged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mentally_challenged "Mentally challenged") man was held by the CIA in order to persuade family members to provide information.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):12[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-New_York_Times2-58) Among the 26 individuals who the CIA acknowledged had been improperly detained, only three were released after less than one month in CIA custody, while most were confined for several months.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1) There is only one example in CIA records of the Agency holding personnel accountable for wrongfully detaining individuals who they themselves determined did not fit MON criteria.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):17 of 499

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Other")]

*   Despite CIA assertions that there were no objections to the interrogation program, some CIA personnel found the torture revolting and asked to be transferred from facilities where torture was being conducted. *   The report suggests torture was the source of a [false confession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_confession "False confession") by [Ibn al-Shaykh al-Libi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_al-Shaykh_al-Libi "Ibn al-Shaykh al-Libi") linking [Saddam Hussein and al-Qaeda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saddam_Hussein_and_al-Qaeda_link_allegations "Saddam Hussein and al-Qaeda link allegations") that was cited in [Colin Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Powell "Colin Powell")'s address to the UN in advance of the 2003 [Iraq War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War "Iraq War").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-TheReportItself-1):141[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate_report_on_CIA_torture#cite_note-IraqJustification-59)
